Microsoft (MSFT) is getting paid for artificial intelligence (AI) agents, software that can finish tasks on its own. The maker of Windows and Microsoft 365 now charges more and more customers for how much work these agents do. This makes me bullish on Microsoft. Its AI push is starting to pay for itself, and the company keeps very high margins even while it spends heavily on data centers. The latest quarter backs that up. Revenue from Azure, Microsoft's cloud platform, grew 48%. The operating margin, the share of sales left after operating costs, reached about 50%. The stock is up 9.7% this year. It is no longer cheap after its rally since June, and AI spending keeps climbing. However, I believe agents give Microsoft a clear way to earn that money back. Microsoft gets paid for AI agents mostly through usage. Copilot, its AI assistant, has mainly been sold as a monthly per-user license, but customers can now also buy credits and pay for the work their agents do. Copilot customers using these credits grew more than 75% in a single quarter, while paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats rose just 5% year-over-year. Get 75% Off TipRanks Premium and unlock powerful investing tools to make smarter, more confident investment decisions Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks The two figures measure different things, but the difference in pace stands out. License sales follow a customer's headcount, while credit sales follow the work agents take on, which can grow much faster. Agent 365, Microsoft's registry for managing a company's agents, now holds more than 50 million agents, up over 30% in one quarter. Foundry, where companies build their own AI apps and agents, passed 120,000 customers, and its revenue more than tripled year-over-year. I think Copilot is a big part of Microsoft's future, because usage keeps climbing. Daily users grew more than fivefold year-over-year, and user satisfaction is at an all-time high. Big companies are buying in, too. The number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats grew more than eightfold in a year, and Volkswagen (VWAGY) has rolled out Copilot to more than 330,000 employees. For Microsoft, more usage now means more revenue. Azure keeps speeding up, and agents are part of the reason, since they need a lot of computing power. Its revenue grew 48% in the September quarter, ahead of what Wall Street expected, helped by Foundry. Management expects 49% to 50% growth in the December quarter, excluding currency effects. Microsoft is also getting more out of its hardware. Copilot workload throughput, meaning how much AI work its systems can process, rose more than 50% in one quarter, which should make each AI task cheaper to run. Microsoft's AI spending is high, but I think it is manageable. The company spent $135.9 billion on capex over the past four quarters, mostly on data centers and chips, and that number is still rising. The risk of overinvesting will always be there. That is why return on invested capital (ROIC) is the number I watch most closely. It shows how much profit a company makes on the money put into its business. Adding up the last four quarters gives Microsoft an ROIC of about 22%, so it earns roughly 22 cents on every dollar invested. That is slightly lower than a year earlier, but returns have improved in each of the last two quarters, so I don't see a red flag during such a big build-out. Microsoft is also careful with cash. Over the past 12 months, it still had about $60 billion of free cash flow, the money left after capex. I usually prefer companies that spend more aggressively, but I understand why Microsoft doesn't want to make its shareholders nervous. In late October, it raised $25 billion in its first major U.S. bond sale since 2017, which gives it more room to keep building data centers without draining its own cash. Management expects free cash flow to stay positive in Fiscal 2027 and says it is confident these investments will pay off over the long run. That convinces me, because agents are already turning part of this spending into revenue. Microsoft stock isn't too expensive, in my view, although it is no longer cheap. Its trailing-12-month (TTM) price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is around 27.7x, based on reported profit, so investors pay about $27.7 for each dollar Microsoft earns in a year. That is higher than the 20.72x it traded at when Fiscal 2026 ended in June, after a sharp sell-off in the first half of the year. Still, it is well below the levels of the three fiscal years before that, when the P/E ended each year above 35x. Looking at the next 12 months, the forward P/E is about 26x, based on analysts' estimates of adjusted earnings, which leave out the impact of Microsoft's investment in OpenAI. I think 26x is a fair price for a company that keeps about half of its sales as operating profit. The main risk is margins. Microsoft's cloud gross margin, the share of cloud revenue left after the direct cost of running it, is already shrinking as lower-margin Azure makes up a bigger part of cloud sales. Management also expects operating margin to dip slightly from a year earlier in the December quarter. If that continues, the stock will start to look expensive. Wall Street sees Microsoft very positively, with a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 35 Buys, four Holds, and zero Sells assigned in the last three months. At $632.48, the average Microsoft price target implies 16.01% upside potential. Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler, one of the top analysts on TipRanks, raised his price target to $722 from $662 after the September-quarter report and reiterated his Outperform (Buy) rating on November 6, implying about 32% upside. He believes lower-than-expected capex and capacity delays created some unwarranted noise around solid results, and I fully agree. I'm bullish on Microsoft. It is spending a lot on AI, and I can already see how that money comes back through agents that customers pay for as they use them. The next test is keeping returns this high while the build-out continues. So far, Microsoft is passing it. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

title: Microsoft’s Neocloud Pullback Isn’t a Crack in AI Demand - MarketBeat
content:
On Nov. 5, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft Corp. NASDAQ: MSFT is stepping away from risky projects with Nebius NASDAQ: NBIS, IREN NASDAQ: IREN and Nscale and debating new neocloud deals. The Financial Times added that Microsoft passed on an option to more than double its Nscale contract in Texas. Those reports, coming on the heels of the U.S. midterm elections, sent neocloud stocks tumbling.  By the end of the day, NBIS was down about 14%, IREN dropped 17%, and CoreWeave NASDAQ: CRWV dropped 10%. Many investors interpreted the news as the first crack in AI demand. The fundamentals tell a different story. Days earlier, Microsoft reported 48% Azure growth and said demand still exceeds supply. Some investors pointed out a less-than-expected capital expenditure (CapEx) number. However, that fell short because third-party suppliers delivered late, not because Microsoft spent less by choice. That context reframes the neocloud news. Bloomberg cited a $1 million fine for unpermitted generators at a New Jersey site being built for Nebius. It also flagged cabling problems at an IREN site in Texas. Microsoft is demanding better execution and building more of its own capacity. Microsoft’s recent moves share a common thread. Each one targets a specific supplier problem. None of them points to weaker demand. For example, a source familiar with the Nscale decision told Reuters that Microsoft made that decision several months ago. The existing Texas contract remains in place. Microsoft declined an expansion option, but it didn't cancel live capacity. The same pattern shows up elsewhere. Microsoft exited an Nscale project in England after grid delays pushed power into the 2030s. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft is winding down a 2023 Oracle deal. The reason given was older NVIDIA chips that no longer meet Microsoft’s specifications. Both of those examples provide nuance to the delays with IREN. On its earnings call, the company communicated that Microsoft requested network design changes that pushed some deliveries into early 2027. The company said it faces no financial penalties for those changes, and that its vertically integrated business model put it in a position to manage the changes in ways that other neoclouds would not be able to do. The numbers from Microsoft’s fiscal first quarter support that reading. Azure revenue grew 48% to $33.2 billion, surpassing management’s guidance of 44% to 45%. Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate to 49% to 50% in the current quarter. Microsoft’s commercial backlog tells a similar story. Remaining performance obligations rose 73% to $677 billion. That represents contracted future revenue that Microsoft has yet to recognize. A company with that backlog cannot afford unreliable suppliers. Investors have seen this movie before. In early 2025, reports that Microsoft was canceling data center leases sparked fears of an AI slowdown. Microsoft’s capital spending kept climbing anyway. There is a tradeoff investors should not ignore. Renting capacity from neoclouds spreads costs over the life of a contract. Building it means paying more up front. If Microsoft owns more capacity, more of the cost lands on its own balance sheet. That cost is already visible. Free cash flow fell about 27% to $18.6 billion last quarter. Operating cash flow rose 29% to $58 billion over the same period. The gap reflects how much cash Microsoft is pouring into data centers. Spending is set to rise from here. CFO Amy Hood guided for CapEx above $50 billion in the December quarter. She also expects spending to accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year. That includes third-party capacity that slipped from earlier quarters. The mix of that spending matters too. Hood said roughly 75% of CapEx now goes to short-lived assets such as GPUs and CPUs. Those chips lose value far faster than buildings do. Owning more of them puts more pressure on future margins. Investors should ask whether “build, don’t rent” means even heavier CapEx ahead. Microsoft hasn’t said how much neocloud capacity it plans to replace with its own. That answer will shape free cash flow for years. For neocloud stocks, the sell-off may not be pure overreaction. Microsoft is a major customer for Nebius, IREN, and Nscale. If it concentrates on fewer suppliers, the risk to those business models is real. Execution now matters as much as headline contract values. IREN’s backlog grew 22% to $20.3 billion last quarter. But the company still needs about $6 billion in financing for its fiscal 2027 spending plan. Delivery delays make that harder. For MSFT shareholders, the picture is more favorable. Demand remains ahead of supply, and Microsoft is using its leverage to secure better capacity. The open question is cost, not demand. Key dates will test the thesis. Nebius reports earnings on Nov. 12. IREN is targeting January 2027 to bring more than $4 billion in contracted annual recurring revenue online, although additional supplier delays could push that milestone into February. Microsoft’s fiscal second-quarter report in late January will show whether CapEx topped $50 billion as promised. Before you consider Microsoft, you'll want to hear this. title: Microsoft Azure Drives Q1 Growth: Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock Now? - TradingView
content: Microsoft MSFT kicked off fiscal 2027 with Azure in the driver’s seat, raising the question of whether investors should buy, sell or hold the stock now. First-quarter fiscal 2027 revenues rose 19% year over year to $92.3 billion, while Microsoft Cloud revenues climbed 30% to $63.9 billion. Azure generated $33.2 billion in revenues, which increased 48% year over year and came ahead of management’s expectations. However, surging capital spending, margin pressure and softness in consumer businesses suggest a balanced approach in the near term. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MSFT’s fiscal 2027 earnings is pegged at $19.87 per share. The estimate indicates 10.7% year-over-year growth. Microsoft Corporation price-consensus-chart | Microsoft Corporation Quote Microsoft’s fundamental appeal rests on its ability to monetize AI across infrastructure, platforms and applications. Foundry revenues more than tripled year over year, aided by GPU fleet efficiency gains and higher revenue per token. Daily Copilot usage rose nearly 50% sequentially and more than fivefold year over year, while customers consuming Copilot credits through usage-based billing grew more than 75%. Average revenue per user is being lifted by premium offerings, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, E5 and E7. Infrastructure execution is also improving. Microsoft added 24 new data centers across five continents during the quarter, cut dock-to-live times for new GB300 systems in its largest regions by about 20% sequentially and docked its first Rubin GPUs. The company completed pre-training of MAI Base 2, its next first-party base model. Still, there are pressure points. Microsoft Cloud gross margin declined to 66% as the mix shifted toward Azure, and commercial bookings fell 12% against a tough prior-year comparison. The Devices and Consumer segment revenues declined 3% to $15.5 billion, as Windows OEM and devices revenues dropped 22% and Xbox content and services revenues slipped 2%. Microsoft’s Azure blog highlights steady product momentum in October and November 2026. In October, Microsoft detailed the architecture of its Maia 300 chip, positioned as a single platform for cloud-scale agentic inference, and introduced the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service in public preview. The company expanded its sovereign cloud and sovereign AI offerings, giving customers greater control over where workloads run. In November, MSFT showcased Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines accelerating electronic design automation workloads and brought fal’s multimodal models to Microsoft Foundry. Microsoft Ignite, scheduled for Nov. 17-20, 2026, is likely to bring additional agent and infrastructure announcements. For the second quarter of fiscal 2027, Microsoft expects revenues between $96 billion and $97.1 billion, indicating 18-19% year-over-year growth. Azure revenue growth is projected to accelerate to 49-50% in constant currency, supported by CPU and GPU fleet efficiencies. Second-quarter operating expense guidance includes the estimated cost of an employee voluntary exit offer. The flip side is spending intensity. First-quarter capital expenditures, including finance leases, were $45.2 billion, with roughly three-fourths allocated to short-lived assets, mainly CPUs and GPUs. Microsoft expects second-quarter capex to exceed $50 billion, bringing projected calendar-year 2026 spending to approximately $170 billion, as demand continues to exceed available capacity. Management expects free cash flow to remain positive throughout fiscal 2027, while the company returned $10.2 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks in the first quarter. MSFT shares have gained 12.8% in the year-to-date (YTD) period compared with the Zacks Computer – Software industry’s 1.6% return. The Zacks Computer and Technology sector has appreciated 7.2% in the same time frame. The stock’s underperformance relative to the broader sector may reflect investor caution over the payback period for heavy AI infrastructure spending. From a valuation standpoint, MSFT stock appears overvalued, trading at a trailing 12-month price/earnings ratio of 30.22X, higher than the industry’s 27.83X. MSFT has a Value Score of C. The premium faces intensifying competition from cloud and AI rivals. Amazon’s AMZN AWS revenues grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter of 2026, and Amazon projects AWS growth exceeding 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Investors can hold Amazon despite its premium valuation, as accelerating AWS growth and expanding operating income support long-term earnings. Alphabet’s GOOGL Google Cloud revenues jumped 103% to $30.7 billion in the third quarter, with Alphabet disclosing a cloud backlog of $561 billion, making Alphabet a fast-rising challenger. Nvidia NVDA posted data center revenues of $89 billion, up 117%, in the second quarter of fiscal 2027. While Nvidia supplies Vera Rubin systems to Azure, Nvidia’s expanding deals with rival clouds intensify the race for scarce AI capacity. Accelerating Azure growth and expanding AI adoption support the long-term case, but elevated capex, margin pressure and a premium valuation suggest existing investors hold while new investors await a better entry point. title: Microsoft Reportedly Pushes Back Against Trump’s Plan To Ban Chinese Optical Transceivers – Flags Challenges To Data Center Rollout - TradingView
content: Microsoft (MSFT) is reportedly urging the Trump administration to abandon a proposed ban on Chinese-made components used in AI data centers, warning that the restrictions could disrupt supply chains and hamper U.S.’ AI buildout. Microsoft is among several companies and trade groups pushing back against the administration’s plans to ban imports of new Chinese optical transceiver models over national security concerns, according to a Reuters report on Tuesday. The devices convert electrical signals into light and back, allowing servers, AI chips and networking equipment to exchange massive amounts of data through fiber-optic cables at high speeds. MSFT shares edged 0.3% lower in pre-market trading. Ban Could Threaten US Data Center Rollout, Says Tech Lobby Microsoft reportedly met with White House and National Security Council officials in September, alongside other technology companies, to highlight potential shortages if the ban takes effect. “It really threatens to arguably grind (the data center rollout) to a halt,” John Miller, general counsel of the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI), told Reuters. ITI, a tech lobbying group, had previously urged the FCC to avoid broad restrictions on optical transceivers. Microsoft currently operates more than 500 data centers across 34 countries. In the U.S., it has 35 under construction and 134 planned, according to Cleanview, as cited in the report. China’s Dominance In Optical Transceiver Market Raises Espionage Concerns The report adds that the U.S. fears the foreign-made components could potentially allow China to steal sensitive information, introduce malicious software, or disrupt U.S. data centers. Chinese companies control roughly two-thirds of the global optical transceiver market, according to Counterpoint Research. The report highlighted Coherent (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE) as competing manufacturers, but added that Western suppliers lack the scale to replace Chinese volume in the near term. The development comes amid heightened scrutiny of Chinese espionage following reports linking Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang to a businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of sharing information with Beijing. On Monday, Trump said Huang denied knowing about the alleged espionage. Nvidia’s board has launched an investigation, while China has rejected the spying allegations. title: Is Microsoft Stock Worth More Than Its Competitors? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Apple is the only stock among a peer group of Alphabet, Amazon, Apple and Salesforce that costs more than Microsoft (MSFT) for each dollar of earnings. Apple trades at 38.7 times earnings, compared with 28.4 for Microsoft. Yet Microsoft keeps a larger share of its sales as operating profit than any of the four, Apple included. So how much more does Microsoft deliver than Apple, at the lower price? Microsoft Beats Apple On Growth And Margin For Less Microsoft grew revenue 17.9% over its latest four fiscal quarters, against 15.1% for Apple over its own. Its operating margin was 47.1%, against 33.0% for Apple. Yet over the year to November 9, 2026, Apple stock returned 30.5% including dividends, against 10.6% for Microsoft. Alphabet is the one peer that grew faster than Microsoft, at 22.2%, and its stock costs just 15.0 times earnings. But Alphabet’s net income over those four quarters was about 1.5 times its operating income, so part of the profit behind that low multiple came from outside its operations. Amazon and Salesforce cost less than Microsoft and grew more slowly. Microsoft’s fastest growth comes from its Intelligent Cloud segment, whose revenue rose 29.7% in fiscal 2026, against 15.9% for Productivity and Business Processes. More Personal Computing, the third segment, shrank 1.1%. Intelligent Cloud made up 41.5% of company revenue in fiscal 2026, up from 37.7% a year earlier. In fiscal Q1 2027, management said Azure revenue rose 48% and that customer demand continues to exceed available supply. Microsoft’s operating margin has widened alongside that growth, rising to 49.8% in fiscal Q1 2027 from 48.9% a year earlier, though management said a shift in sales toward Azure partly offset that gain. Its operating margin over the past four quarters is the highest such figure at any of the 40 quarter ends since fiscal Q2 2017. Management expects growth to hold, projecting revenue growth of 18% to 19% for fiscal Q2 2027 and Azure growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency. Microsoft reported revenue growth of 18.8% for fiscal Q1 2027. Microsoft is paying for that growth in cash. Its free cash flow in fiscal Q1 2027 was about 28% below a year earlier, even as cash from operations rose 29%. Management said the lower free cash flow reflects higher capital spending. Management expects that spending to accelerate in the second half of fiscal 2027, partly because some capacity it was counting on for fiscal Q2 2027 moved into that half. Management also expects Microsoft to remain free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027. Microsoft already delivers more than Apple, the one peer priced higher, on both growth and margin. At its price, you are paying for Microsoft to keep growing at about its current pace and to hold its margin while its spending climbs. Its latest quarter did both. Revenue growth and free cash flow in Microsoft’s January 2027 report are the numbers to watch. You don’t have to bet on one stock to earn. content: Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) shares surged 2.34% to $543.03 on Monday, gaining $12.42 amid strong buying momentum. The stock approached an intraday high near $546. Meanwhile, Northern Trust announced an expanded Microsoft partnership focused on institutional client onboarding. Northern Trust introduced an AI-powered onboarding agent for its Front Office Solutions platform. The companies developed the system through their engineering teams to simplify complex investment data processing. The project extends their collaboration into asset servicing operations. Front Office Solutions supports foundations, pension funds, endowments, and large family offices. These clients often maintain transaction records across systems. Consequently, onboarding teams must organize historical data before the platform can generate consistent performance reports. Alternative investments add complexity because their records require reconstruction. Northern Trust’s survey found that 57% of asset owners identified fragmented data consolidation as their leading challenge. The new agent addresses that problem by converting client transaction histories into a standard reporting format. Northern Trust reported that the agent reduced data preparation time from two and a half weeks to three days. That change represents an 83% reduction in the measured process. The company also reported a 96.5% first-pass F1 score for the system’s output. The F1 measure combines precision and recall to assess the quality of automated results. However, Northern Trust analysts still review the agent’s decisions and correct exceptions. This process helps teams identify errors before clients begin using the reporting platform. The system operates on Microsoft Azure and uses Microsoft Foundry. It also connects with Excel and SharePoint, providing tools for approval. Meanwhile, a governed knowledge layer retains approved onboarding information to support future work. Microsoft and Northern Trust designed the system around financial services privacy and governance requirements. Microsoft evaluated performance with anonymized data while Northern Trust retained control of client information. This approach allowed the engineering teams to improve results without exposing clients’ underlying records. The firms also built human oversight into the workflow rather than removing analysts from decisions. Northern Trust expects automation to reduce repetitive preparation work and create more time for specialized tasks. Its strategy combines automated processing with staff judgment across sensitive client operations. The announcement illustrates Microsoft’s push to apply enterprise AI within heavily regulated financial institutions. For Northern Trust, the rollout targets an operational bottleneck that affects onboarding speed and reporting readiness. title: Microsoft (MSFT.US) Reportedly Plans to Reduce Reliance on Neoclouds Amid Resistance to AI Infrastructure Expansion - 富途牛牛
content: According to CNBC, citing people familiar with the matter, Microsoft (MSFT.US) is reducing its neocloud partner list, focusing on collaboration with a select few major vendors, and expanding its own data centers. The plan poses another potential challenge for certain segments of the artificial intelligence market. With borrowing costs rising, heavy debt burdens, and market concerns that the pace of infrastructure expansion may slow, related industries are already showing signs of strain. In recent years, Microsoft has established cooperative relationships with several neocloud companies, including CoreWeave (CRWV.US), Nebius (NBIS.US), Chronoscale (CHRN.US), IREN (IREN.US), Lambda, Nscale, and Oracle (ORCL.US), which is making substantial investments in AI infrastructure. Two sources said Microsoft is still in the evaluation phase and has not yet decided which neoclouds to discontinue. One of them noted that Microsoft aims to prioritize expanding its own data center infrastructure. Bloomberg had earlier reported on these plans. Additionally, two other sources stated that Microsoft has chosen not to renew its cooperation agreement with Oracle. A Microsoft spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its infrastructure strategy "is built on flexibility and choice." The spokesperson said, "We combine Microsoft's own data centers, leased facilities, and strategic partnerships with third-party vendors to provide the required capacity where and when our customers need it. We regularly review these investments in line with customer demand, including tracking delivery progress and adjusting plans as circumstances change." In recent weeks, neocloud-related stocks have been volatile on Wall Street. Rising interest rates have heightened market concerns about companies' rapid capacity expansion and over-reliance on debt. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN have all fallen by about half over the past month, even after a rebound last Friday (the 6th). A recent industry study found that there are currently 323 neocloud companies, and experts predict that many of them will struggle to survive. IREN said when it announced its results last Thursday that it had delivered data center capacity to Microsoft in August, but Microsoft requested an upgrade of network equipment, causing the related infrastructure to be commissioned in January or February next year instead of within this year. During the company's fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings call in October, Microsoft CFO Amy Hood stated that some cloud contracts involving graphics processors have been delayed until the first half of 2027, impacting the growth of Azure's cloud business. Microsoft's latest quarterly capital expenditures and finance leases totaled $45.2 billion, and the company indicated that capital spending will accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year. CoreWeave and Nebius are set to release their quarterly results. IREN's shares surged 16% last Friday after the company reported that AI revenue more than doubled quarter-over-quarter to $200 million. IREN Co-CEO Daniel Roberts told CNBC, "There is a disconnect between what we see in the public markets and at the client level." However, he acknowledged that the market environment poses challenges. Roberts said on the earnings call, "Capital markets have become more selective over the past few weeks, and market focus has undoubtedly shifted from contract size to delivery capability, financing, and profitability." Microsoft had earlier scaled back its partnership with the UK's neocloud Nscale, abandoning a planned site in England. In October, Darren Hardman, Microsoft's president for the UK and Ireland, told CNBC that the decision was related to Nscale's ability to secure power supply. The Financial Times reported this week that Microsoft has decided not to renew Nscale's contract in Texas. Nscale filed for an IPO in mid-September but has not updated its prospectus since. In its IPO filing, the company stated that it expected Microsoft to become a "significant customer" in the future. Microsoft's major shift to CoreWeave began after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, when demand for GPUs surged. In search of alternative supply sources, Microsoft partnered with CoreWeave, which was still privately held at the time and originated from cryptocurrency mining operations. When CoreWeave went public last year, it stated that 62% of its 2024 revenue would come from Microsoft. When ChatGPT launched, OpenAI used only Azure. Its current cloud providers also include Amazon (AMZN.US), Cerebras (CBRS.US), CoreWeave, Google, and Oracle. A Microsoft spokesperson said that reviewing the neocloud investment is a "normal and responsible way to manage large, complex infrastructure projects," adding that "the pace of the new agreement reflects current actual needs." title: Microsoft's (NASDAQ: MSFT) $677 Billion Backlog Signals AI Ambition As Capex Surges And Neocloud Ties Fray - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 8, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) has accumulated remaining performance obligations of $677 billion, a 73% year-over-year jump that reflects the extraordinary scale of enterprise AI commitments flowing into its Azure platform. Roughly 30% of those committed revenues are expected to convert into recognized sales within the next 12 months, underscoring the near-term weight of that backlog on future earnings. Yet the financial picture is more complicated beneath that headline figure, with free cash flow dropping approximately 23% even as adjusted earnings per share climbed 18% year over year. Capital expenditures hit $45.2 billion in the most recent quarter, and management has guided for spending to climb further, to $50 billion, in the second quarter. To help fund that buildout, Microsoft moved quickly to tap debt markets, agreeing to sell $25 billion in notes, the majority of which are earmarked for data center construction and expansion. The company also carried roughly $365 billion in data center leases that had not yet commenced as of September, a figure that illustrates how far forward Microsoft has committed its infrastructure spending. Against that backdrop of accelerating internal investment, reports emerged on Nov. 5 that Microsoft has been tightening oversight of arrangements with neocloud operators, firms that rent out AI computing capacity, including Nebius Group, IREN (NASDAQ: IREN), and the privately held Nscale. Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is pulling back from neocloud projects it considers risky, with the Financial Times adding that the company will not exercise an option to more than double the scale of its Nscale arrangement at a Texas data center. Microsoft has not confirmed either report, but the strategic logic is straightforward: neocloud operators can introduce delays, power constraints, and older chip generations that make AI capital spending harder to predict and control. By bringing more buildout inside its own infrastructure program, Microsoft can align capacity decisions more tightly with its bond-funded expansion and internal return requirements, reducing dependence on third-party timelines. Bookings told a more cautious story during the period, falling 12%, a divergence from the RPO surge that suggests some near-term deal flow softness even as long-term commitments pile up. The stock was trading near $535 at the time of writing, sitting about 4% below a recent high, a level that some analysts consider still elevated relative to the underlying cash flow trajectory. One market observer noted a preference for entering a position closer to $465, suggesting the current price leaves limited margin of safety given the ongoing free cash flow compression. With capex set to keep climbing and the neocloud retreat still unfolding, investors face a company at a pivotal inflection point between enormous long-run AI potential and significant near-term financial strain. title: Rising Rates Cleave AI Infrastructure Stocks (NASDAQ: CRWV, NBIS, MSFT, MU) Into Winners And Losers - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 8, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A widening chasm has opened inside the AI infrastructure sector, and the dividing line is not technology but balance sheets and the cost of borrowed money. With the Federal Reserve holding its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00% and markets pricing in a 72% chance of another quarter-point hike in December, debt-heavy data center builders are absorbing punishment that cash-rich rivals are largely avoiding. The numbers tell the story bluntly: CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) lost 47.54% of its market value in the single month ending November 6, while Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) shed 45.4% over the same stretch. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), which has not yet tapped the debt markets according to CFO Amy Hood, edged 0.16% higher across that same period, a near-perfect illustration of the divergence now reshaping the sector. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh captured the underlying dynamic during a late-October address, warning that “interest rates get in the cracks,” before adding that “interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything,” including the trillion-dollar AI buildout financed heavily with borrowed capital. Long-term borrowing costs are amplifying the Federal Reserve’s pressure from above, with the 10-year Treasury yield reaching 5.24% on October 9 and still sitting at 4.84% on November 5, the same day the VIX volatility index climbed to 28.18, its highest level since early August. CoreWeave’s financial structure illustrates the vulnerability most starkly, with debt running at 8.94 times equity and second-quarter interest expense hitting $640 million, more than double the $267 million recorded a year earlier. The company has guided for $860 million to $940 million in third-quarter interest expense alone, even as it plans to deploy $35 billion to $39 billion in capital spending this year against a revenue backlog of $104.2 billion. Nebius faces a comparable squeeze, having sold $4.34 billion in convertible notes during the first half of the year to help finance $20 billion to $25 billion in planned capital expenditure, with three customers accounting for 24%, 21%, and 14% of its second-quarter revenue, concentrating risk dangerously. Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) sits on $664 billion in signed future revenue but burned $5.4 billion in free cash flow last quarter while capex hit $28.5 billion and interest expense surged 55%, prompting CFO Hilary Maxson to acknowledge that the company has “not given a particular time frame on that yet” for when free cash flow turns positive, as the stock falls 39.64% for the year. Microsoft’s $18.6 billion in quarterly free cash flow, generated even after $45.2 billion in capital spending, positions it as the clearest beneficiary of the current environment, while Alphabet moves in the opposite direction, recording negative $9.07 billion in free cash flow after $51.36 billion in capex and raising $28.7 billion through new bond issuance. Even companies with strong cash generation are not immune, as Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) demonstrates, with its stock dropping 36.57% over the past month despite producing $62.3 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2026. Micron’s exposure stems from its customers, specifically the high-bandwidth memory buyers who are the same debt-dependent data center operators now facing tighter financing conditions, meaning demand for Micron’s chips could soften even without any chip-supply problem. Investors watching for early signals of stress should focus on CoreWeave’s upcoming third-quarter earnings report, where interest expense at or above the top of guidance would confirm that borrowing costs are already constraining the company’s growth trajectory. The Federal Reserve’s December meeting then becomes the next critical inflection point, since another rate increase would raise financing costs on data center contracts structured when capital was substantially cheaper than it is today. title: Berkshire Earnings Drop As Market Seeks Repair, Sandisk And Micron Crumble While Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) And Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Hold Firm - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 8, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK-B) reported a decline in earnings, adding fresh pressure to an equity market already struggling to find stable footing heading into the new trading week. The broader market is in a damaged state, with investors navigating a landscape where former high-performing names have lost significant ground and the path to recovery remains unclear. Dow Jones futures are set to draw close attention from traders on Monday morning after the index shed 0.46% in recent sessions, signaling continued unease across blue-chip holdings. Among the hardest-hit names, Sandisk and Micron have emerged as cautionary examples, with analysts characterizing both stocks as broken rather than merely pulled back from highs. The semiconductor and storage sectors have faced particular scrutiny, as the deterioration in Sandisk and Micron reflects broader concerns about demand cycles and inventory pressures weighing on the industry. Not every corner of the market is in retreat, however, with several mega-cap technology names demonstrating a resilience that stands in contrast to the broader selling pressure. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), which slipped just 0.44%, has managed to hold its ground relative to more battered peers, a sign that investor confidence in the consumer electronics giant remains comparatively intact. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) also showed relative strength with a modest decline of 0.14%, suggesting that its diversified revenue streams across retail and cloud computing continue to attract defensive positioning from institutional buyers. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) dipped 0.85% but is still considered among the names holding up, as its enterprise software and artificial intelligence investments provide a degree of earnings visibility that the market continues to value. The divergence between resilient mega-caps and broken growth names underscores a broader rotation dynamic, where investors are gravitating toward companies with durable cash flows and retreating from those with shakier demand outlooks. Berkshire’s earnings decline is particularly notable given Warren Buffett’s conglomerate is often viewed as a bellwether for Main Street economic conditions, and weakness there may signal softening activity beyond just technology and semiconductors. With the market in need of repair and several key charts compromised, the coming week’s trading session will be critical in determining whether buyers are willing to step in or whether further deterioration lies ahead. title: Berkshire Hathaway Profit Slides As Tech Giants Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), And Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Offer Wall Street A Rare Bright Spot - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 7, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Berkshire Hathaway’s earnings declined in the latest reporting period, adding pressure to an already fragile broader market that analysts say is in need of meaningful repair. The conglomerate’s profit drop stands in contrast to the relative resilience shown by three of the market’s most closely watched technology names heading into the weekend session. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) have each managed to hold their ground, offering investors some reassurance amid a generally unsettled trading environment. Microsoft slipped 0.85% and Apple edged down 0.44%, but both stocks are broadly considered to be weathering current conditions better than much of the rest of the market. The Dow Jones Industrial Average futures pointed lower, with the index off 0.46%, underscoring the cautious tone that has defined recent sessions. While large-cap technology is providing a degree of stability, conditions in the semiconductor space tell a sharply different story, with Micron (NASDAQ: MU) and SanDisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) both described as appearing technically broken. Despite that characterization, Micron actually gained 5.85% and SanDisk rose 4.34% in recent trading, though those moves have done little to alter the underlying technical damage both stocks have sustained. The divergence between short-term price pops and deteriorating chart structures in chip stocks reflects a broader tension running through the current market, where individual sessions can mislead about the health of a trend. Analysts tracking market internals have flagged the need for a sustained period of constructive price action before the broader indexes can be considered to be on solid footing again. The combination of weakening earnings from a bellwether like Berkshire, a shaky technical backdrop for semiconductor names, and index-level softness suggests the path to recovery will require patience from investors rather than a quick rebound. With large-cap technology stocks serving as one of the few dependable pillars of support, the market’s near-term direction may hinge heavily on whether Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft can maintain their current levels through continued volatility. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.
